newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa Naidoo says Telecommunication bill urgent.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa Naidoo says Telecommunication bill urgent.

text.p: South African Telecommunications Minister Jay Naidoo, fielding comments on a wide-ranging draft law on regulatory mechanisms, on Wednesday rejected opposition calls to delay its passage until next year.
Naidoo said the Telecommunications Bill was essential to the government's search for a strategic equity partner for the state-owned Telkom SA telephone company.
"The matter is very urgent," Naidoo said at a parliamentary hearing on the bill, which recently he called the most important telecommunications legislation in 40 years.
"Any delays in this process will have a substantial impact by creating uncertainty in potentially some of the biggest investment into the broader economy," he said.
Opposition National Party and Democratic Party legislators have asked for time to study the bill and to consider extensive but largely technical industry proposals for amendments.

The bill defines a framework for an overhaul of the telecommunications industry, including the five to six billion rand ($1.1-1.3 billion) sale of up to 30 percent of Telkom to one or more foreign investors.

Naidoo last week short-listed seven potential partners for Telkom and set an April deadline for conclusion of the deal. He said an additional 10 percent of Telkom's equity would be set aside for a domestic black empowerment programme.
He said South Africa would encourage the candidates from Germany, France, the Netherlands, Malaysia, the U.S., Italy and Sweden to refine their bids in consortia.

Urging parliament to approve the bill setting up a South African Telecommunications Regulatory Authority and a Universal Service Agency, Naidoo said potential partners needed to know what obligations they would assume and what protection they would have.

Citing examples of countries that have granted between eight and 35 years of exclusivity, he said the bill's provision for a guaranteed monopoly - likely to be between four and six years - in the operation of land-based telephone services was vital to the search for a new investor.

"Certainty in the regulatory environment is crucial to the broader process of restructuring of telecommunications and particularly to the process of finding a strategic equity partner for Telkom," Naidoo said.

Telkom chief executive officer Brian Clark defended the exclusivity proposal, saying it would enable Telkom and its new partners to install telephones in black areas disadvantaged under apartheid before it had to face full competition.
"Telkom recognises the value of competition, but the challenge of having to rapidly expand and modernise the network puts us in a unique situation," he said.
Clark said Telkom was committed to effectively double the telephone network by installing three million new lines and modernising a million more within five years.

Vodacom, one of South Africa's two cellular telephone networks, argued against a provision requiring all licenced telephone operators to contribute to a Universal Service Fund to help eliminate the black backlog in telephone services.
"We take the view that the imposition of what are tantamount to additional licence fees on our National Telecommunications Licence is unacceptable," the company said in written testimony.

Vodacom said it negotiated a licence at 100 million rand a year plus five percent of operating income and was already paying 20 million rand a year more than expected because of the success of the system.
Rival cellular operator MTN argued that the existing contractual contribution to infrastructure in deprived areas should be assessed as a contribution in kind to the Universal Service Fund.
